The Eye.
Many Greenland sharks swim around with a small crustacean hanging off the front of one eyeball.
It's a parasitic copepod, a distant relative of shrimp about three centimeters long,
and the female grips the clear surface of the eye, anchors herself into it, and stays there.
Researchers who studied infected eyes from the Canadian Arctic found scarring at every anchor point,
and they warned that it could badly damage the shark's vision.
So for decades, the Greenland shark was often called blind.
Here's the twist: in twenty twenty-six, a team led from the University of California, Irvine
published a close look inside eyes from sharks caught off western Greenland.
The light-sensing layer at the back showed no signs of wearing out,
even in sharks estimated at more than a hundred years old.
The parasites didn't seem to stop the eyes working.
Its retina is built for dim light and is tuned to the blue that reaches the deep,
so a shark with a passenger on its eyeball still gets around.
That's like letting a stranger sit on your windscreen for years and driving to work anyway.

The Pup.
Almost everything known about how a Greenland shark is born comes from one pregnant female,
reported in nineteen fifty-seven.
She was about five meters long, and inside her were ten pups close to birth,
each about thirty-seven centimeters.
A twenty twenty review of the species' breeding called her
the only confirmed pregnant Greenland shark in the scientific record.
It's like trying to understand how humans are born from one hospital note written in nineteen fifty-seven.
The strange part is how little has been added since.
Scientists estimate that a newborn is somewhere between thirty-five and forty-five centimeters long,
based on the size of the eggs, but that's a calculation, not a sighting.
Even that one record is shaky, because the reviewers suspect she may have lost some pups when she was caught,
so ten might not be the real number.
Nobody knows how long the pregnancy lasts.
The same review listed finding the places where pups are born and raised as work that still needs doing.
So somewhere in the Arctic, the longest-living vertebrate known
starts its life in a nursery that nobody has ever found.

The Growth.
A Greenland shark grows less than one centimeter a year.
That number goes back to a medium-sized shark tagged off Greenland in the nineteen thirties.

it had grown by only a few centimeters in total.
It would take a completely different method, decades later, to work out how old these sharks actually get.
Here's the problem: your fingernails grow about four centimeters a year,
which is more than four times faster than this shark.
Now put that pace next to its size. A big Greenland shark can be five meters long.
At less than a centimeter a year, a body that size is not built in a decade, or even in a century.
This isn't a sick or hungry shark,

Greenland sharks live in seas that can be as cold as minus two degrees Celsius,

The Slowest Shark.
When scientists tagged six Greenland sharks,
their usual cruising speed came out at about one point two kilometers an hour.
That's less than a third of a normal walking pace.
One full sweep of the tail can take about seven seconds,
and even its fastest burst in that study stayed under three kilometers an hour.
For a fish of its size, nothing measured has been slower,
and the researchers who tagged it pointed to the cold water it lives in as the likely reason.

The Menu.
One Greenland shark was reportedly found with a whole reindeer inside it.
Other reports mention parts of a horse,
and one scientific survey of their stomachs found the remains of a polar bear.
These are land animals, and this shark lives in the sea,
often hundreds of meters down in near-freezing water.
Nobody has shown it hunting any of them,
but it's a known scavenger that eats whatever comes down to meet it,
including leftover whale meat that whalers near Svalbard threw back.
It's also very good at finding whatever comes down:
in one Canadian Arctic study, researchers lowered squid-baited cameras into deep water,
and Greenland sharks showed up at eight out of every ten.

The Meat.
Fresh Greenland shark is poisonous to eat.
Its flesh is loaded with urea and a chemical called trimethylamine oxide,
and eaten fresh, it's considered hazardous.
In Iceland, people found a way around it:
they ferment the meat first,
then hang it up to dry,
and the result is called hákarl, which is still eaten there today.
Here's the interesting part: in one study by Icelandic food scientists,
the meat was fermented for about eight weeks and then dried for five more.
Within five weeks of fermenting, the problem chemical had dropped below the level their tests could detect.
It's a sandwich you have to leave alone for about three months before anyone will eat it,
which is the exact opposite of how sandwiches work.
Iceland isn't hunting these sharks for it, either.

The Teenager.
A female Greenland shark may not be ready to breed until she's around a hundred and fifty years old.
Females are thought to mature at around four meters long.

so the exact number may still move.

The Deep.
Greenland sharks have been recorded as deep as about two thousand two hundred meters.
They live in water close to freezing,
and that cold is the main idea for why they live so long.
A cold body means a slow metabolism,
and a slow metabolism may mean less wear and tear on the tissues over the years.
It's a body kept on a fridge shelf for its entire life.
The strange part is in its genes:
in twenty twenty-four, researchers released the first full Greenland shark genome as a preprint,
and it is about twice as long as ours.
More than seventy percent of it is made of repeating stretches sometimes called jumping genes,
and many of its duplicated genes are involved in repairing damaged DNA.
One of the body's main anti-cancer proteins also carries a change the team wants to study further.
